blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today we have two surprises for you: a giant octopus that swims through the sky, and a river giant that makes its own sunscreen.
Ready?
Let's go!
First, let's look up at the sky.
At a giant kite festival, thousands of kites fill the air.
There are dragons and whales, sea turtles and astronauts, all floating high above the ground.
But the biggest star of the show is an octopus — a giant octopus kite!
One famous octopus kite is eighty meters long.
That is longer than two blue whales, nose to tail!
It took its maker six months to finish.
It is so big that a team of at least six people must work together to fly it.
At minimum, six people hold the lines, and sometimes they even need a car to pull it into the air!
When the wind catches it, the long arms wave and dance, and the whole sky turns into a colorful curtain.
Visitors look up and yell with joy.
In total, a big festival can fill the sky with thousands of kites, and people come from many countries just to watch.
A small standard kite fits in your hand, but these giants need a whole team — and a lot of sky!
Now let's dive into the river and meet a very big animal with a very strange secret: the hippopotamus.
When a hippo comes out of the water on a sunny day, its skin slowly turns pink.
For a long time, people thought hippos sweated blood!
Let me clarify: it is not blood, and it is not really sweat, either.
Hippos do not have sweat glands like we do.
Instead, tiny glands under their skin make a clear, oily fluid.
In just a few minutes in the air and sun, the fluid turns pink and then red.
Scientists found two special pigments inside it: a red one called hipposudoric acid, and an orange one called norhipposudoric acid.
Together, they work like a natural sunscreen.
They soak up the sun's ultraviolet rays, so the hippo's sensitive skin does not burn.
The same fluid also fights bacteria, so small cuts from life in a muddy river do not easily get infected.
And because it is oily, it keeps the skin soft and wet, like a built-in moisturizer.
Hippos spend most of the day in the water to stay cool.
But when they come out onto the bank in the sun, their own pink sunscreen is already on the job.
You have to appreciate how clever nature is!
Here's today's idiom: 'rain cats and dogs.' When it rains cats and dogs, it rains very, very heavily!

Here's an example: 'We wanted to fly our kites at the festival, but it rained cats and dogs, so we waited under a big tent.' No cats or dogs really fall from the sky — it is just a fun way to say the rain is pouring down!
Let's think about our stories: a giant octopus kite that needs a whole team, and a hippo that makes its own sunscreen.
First: if you could design any giant kite, what animal or shape would you pick?
Second: the hippo's pink fluid does three jobs at once — can you think of another animal with a clever trick like that?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Keep looking up, keep wondering, and may your next rainy day never rain cats and dogs — unless you love puddles!
See you tomorrow!
